definition: Techniques for combining the weights of multiple trained models (often fine-tuned variants of the same base model) into a single model without additional training.
details: Model merging methods, such as weight averaging or task-vector arithmetic, can combine capabilities from multiple specialized fine-tunes into one model at little to no additional training cost.

explainer.lead: Model merging combines the weights of several trained models, often fine-tuned variants of one base model, into a single model without further training. It lets teams assemble capabilities from several specialized fine-tunes at little or no extra training cost.

tiers.eli5: It is like blending several already-cooked sauces into one pot instead of cooking a new dish from scratch.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers merge weight averages or task vectors from specialized fine-tunes rather than retraining. A pitfall is that merging models with divergent fine-tuning can degrade some capabilities, so merged results need evaluation.
tiers.paperLevel: Methods such as weight averaging and task-vector arithmetic combine parameters directly; success depends on the fine-tunes sharing a common base and on task vectors being compatible. Known limits: conflicts between task vectors can cause interference and lost performance.

explainer.example: Two fine-tunes of the same base model, one for coding and one for summarization, are merged by averaging weights into one model that handles both tasks without retraining.
